Leveraging Online Learning for Domain-Adaptation
in Wi-Fi-based Device-Free Localization
Jie Zhang, Member, IEEE, Jianqiang Xue, Yanjiao Li, Member, IEEE,
and Simon L. Cotton, Fellow, IEEE
Abstract—Wi-Fi-based device-free localization (DFL) will be
an integral part of many emerging applications, such as smart
healthcare and smart homes. One popular approach to DFL
in Wi-Fi makes use of fingerprinting based on channel state
information (CSI). Unfortunately, high-quality fingerprints can-
not easily be obtained in many real-world environments due to
the complicated, time-varying and multipath conditions which
exist. Additionally, existing methods struggle to update the DFL
models in a real-time manner to track changes of environment.
To address these issues, an online data-driven modelling DFL
framework is designed for robustness enhancement. Specifically,
the raw CSI data is first augmented with the hidden layer
parameters of an online deep neural network to strengthen the
pair-to-pair mappings between signal variations and a target’s
location. The radio map created with the augmented fingerprints
can be updated with new sequential data collected from other
domains, such as different times and layouts of the same envi-
ronment. Subsequently, a novel online DFL model is established
using these augmented fingerprints, which itself can be updated
with new sequential data from other domains without the need
for retraining. A forgetting mechanism is considered to mitigate
the effects of outdated data on the localization performance. To
validate our new framework, a comprehensive set of experiments
have been performed in various environments for different
scenarios. The experimental results verify the robustness and
responsive tracking ability of the proposed online data-driven
modelling DFL framework.
Index Terms—Device-free localization, fingerprint augmenta-
tion, fingerprint vanishing, online deep learning.

However, these methods usually require a device to be carried
or worn by the user (target), or they present significant privacy
concerns, and in the case of camera-based systems do not
function well in poorly illuminated environments [7], [8]. Over
the last decade, advances in contactless sensing, utilizing the
ubiquity of Wi-Fi signals, has demonstrated its potential to
estimate a target’s location without many of the drawbacks
listed above. This approach to positioning estimation is often
referred to as device-free localization (DFL) [9]–[13]. Since
it is well-known that human activity is strongly correlated
with changes in the characteristics of wireless channels [14]–
[16], this lends itself to the opportunity to perform human
activity recognition. Physiological parameters like respiration,
as well as movements (e.g., walking, running and falling) and
location, can be inferred by analyzing fluctuations of channel
state information (CSI) and received signal strength (RSS),
both of which can be easily extracted from commodity Wi-Fi
devices [17]–[20].
Existing Wi-Fi-based DFL methods can be broadly divided
into data-driven methods and model-based methods. Data-
driven methods usually build the relationship between the tar-
get’s location and signal pattern with the help of machine/deep
learning, while model-based methods prefer to explore the
physical meaning and mathematical relationship between the
environment, target’s location and signal variation [21]–[24].
However, most existing DFL methods cannot address one of
the most fundamental challenges when they are deployed in
real-world settings. More precisely, Wi-Fi signals characterize
both the target’s location and physical environment due to the
nature of the wireless signal propagation, thus data collected
from commodity Wi-Fi devices carries environmental infor-
mation unrelated to the target’s location, which may degrade
the localization performance [25]–[27]. Moreover, different
body shapes can impact Wi-Fi signals in different ways, even
though the target is at the same location. A small domain
shift may cause serious performance degradation of high-
accuracy DFL systems [28]–[30]. When a “good” DFL model
is built for a specific domain, it may fail to achieve comparable
localization performance in terms of accuracy and robustness
in other domains. One possible way to tackle this issue is
to build different DFL models for each new domain, but
model retraining and rebuilding are usually time-consuming
and labor-intensive [31]–[34]. Therefore, how to achieve satis-
factory performance under environmental variations is the key
to reduce the gap between the systems demonstrated within
carefully controlled laboratory settings and systems deployed


2
in real-world scenarios [35]–[37].
Considering the above limitations, this study aims to de-
velop a novel framework for DFL with domain-adaptation
ability, whereby once it is built for a specific domain it can be
transferred to other domains with minimal overheads while
still retaining its localization performance. To create such
a domain-adaptation DFL framework, two major obstacles
need to be overcome [38]. The first issue is that primitive
features, such as the CSI amplitude and phase used in existing
works, are sensitive to the environmental variations. This leads
to the poor robustness when using a DFL model created
for one domain in a different domain. The second is that
training a DFL model with good domain-adaptation ability
usually needs sophisticated machine/deep learning algorithms
with a complicated architecture and large number of tuned
parameters. This typically hinders the large-scale deployment
of DFL systems.
This work focuses on addressing the above two challenges
to build a fast and robust DFL framework based on online
data-driven modelling, which comprises two steps, namely
fingerprint augmentation and online modelling. To be specific,
in the fingerprint augmentation step, an online sequential
multilayer extreme learning machine (OS-ML-ELM), a series
of stacked online autoencoders (AE) without an iterative
mechanism in its training process, is first employed to map the
raw CSI data to another feature space to alleviate the effects
of environmental variations and multipath on the localization
performance, i.e., using the hidden layer parameters of OS-
ML-ELM as a replacement for raw fingerprints to construct
an augmented radio map. The augmented radio map can be
directly updated using OS-ML-ELM without the need for
retraining to track the environmental variations. In real-world
scenarios, the sequentially collected channel data is usually
spatially and time correlated. This means that recently col-
lected samples will usually better represent the current domain,
while the outdated data will often make less contribution to
the model updating. Therefore, in the online modelling step, a
modified online modelling algorithm, named online sequential
extreme learning machine with forgetting factor embedding
(OS-ELM-FF), is then developed for domain-adaptation ability
enhancement. The main advantages of the proposed online
data-driven modelling DFL framework are multi-fold:
• Considering that primitive features, such as the CSI
amplitude and phase, are sensitive to the environmental
variations and multipath, a novel fingerprint augmentation
method is developed based on OS-ML-ELM to use the
hidden layer parameters as a new type of fingerprint
to better represent the target’s location. Unlike existing
hierarchical neural networks, where all the hidden layers
are treated as a whole system, each hidden layer of OS-
ML-ELM is an independent module. Once the fingerprint
of the previous hidden layer is augmented, the weights
or parameters of the current hidden layer will be fixed,
and need not to be fine-tuned. Therefore, the training of
OS-ML-ELM and updating of the constructed radio map
will be much faster. This makes the radio map constructed
for the source domain readily transferable to other target
domains.
• A novel OS-ELM-FF-based DFL model is developed to
enhance the cross-domain localization performance under
environmental variations. Different from existing DFL
models, it can be updated using the augmented finger-
prints from new domains without retraining. Moreover,
the embedded forgetting mechanism reduces the effects
of outdated data on the localization performance and
accelerates model updating.
• The proposed online data-driven modelling DFL frame-
work was implemented using commodity Wi-Fi devices
in different indoor environments. We verified the pro-
posed framework in various scenarios, including using
data collected at different times, different body shapes
of targets, different Wi-Fi device positions and heights,
and layout changes of testbed, etc. Experimental results
demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the pro-
posed framework in real indoor settings.

II. RELATED WORK
In this section, we briefly review recent advances in domain-
independent human activity recognition and transfer learning-
based domain-adaptation DFL using commodity Wi-Fi de-
vices.
A. Wi-Fi-based Domain-Independent Contactless Human Ac-
tivity Recognition
Wi-Fi-based contactless human activity recognition is be-
coming an attractive area of research driven in part by new
applications in smart healthcare and smart homes [39]. It
works by learning high-level information of human behaviors
from the raw data collected by Wi-Fi infrastructure. Prior
works assume that all the data used in the human activity
recognition follows similar distributions, resulting in the poor
robustness and generalization when the proposed methods
are implemented in new domains. Recent advances primarily
resort to transfer learning, adversarial learning, or novel fea-
ture representation to address the domain-dependent problem.
For instance, EI [32] was designed based on an adversarial
network, which could remove the environment and subject
specific information, and extract domain-independent features.
Widar3.0 [40] first proposed a domain-independent feature,
and then trained a “one-fits-all” model using deep neural
networks for capturing the spatial-temporal characteristics of
human gestures. HandGest [41] first designed two modified
features from the hand-oriented view, and then developed a
hierarchical framework to achieve robust handwriting recog-
nition, even under significant changes of locations of Wi-Fi
devices, drawing sizes, or initial locations of the hand. Wang
et al. [42] proposed a scenario transferring network to generate


3
virtual data using data collected from both the current scenario
and another available scenario with the aim of enhancing the
quality of the synthesized data learned from the other scenario.
They also developed a novel deep adversarial network to guide
features of the target scenario shift to those of the source
scenario in an unsupervised manner for cross-scenario human
activity recognition [43].
B. Transfer Learning for Domain-Adaptation DFL
Transfer learning has the potential to transfer knowledge
from a well-labeled domain (i.e., source domain) to an unla-
beled domain (i.e., target domain) [44]. The essence of transfer
learning is to find an equivalent transformation to minimize the
distance between the source domain and target domain. Several
transfer learning methods have been proposed and successfully
implemented for DFL. Wang et al. [45] designed a novel
DFL scheme to process RSS measurements and determine
the differential RSS of two adjacent time instants to estimate
the target’s location. This procedure eliminates the need to
acquire reference RSS measurements and alleviates the effect
of the surrounding environment. Ohara et al. [46] successfully
transferred a signal strength model from the source domain
to the target domain. However, the proposed method requires
that the link lengths remain consistent across different envi-
ronments, limiting its range of potential applications. Chang
et al. [47] designed a low-cost DFL system, named FitLoc,
for estimating the location of multiple targets. This reduces
the cost associated with transferring the radio map between
the source environment and target environment. As the radio
map construction of the source environment required for
FitLoc is time-consuming, DTransfer [48] was developed.
In this approach, an optimized low-rank matrix completion
model was proposed for efficient radio map construction. Chen
et al. [49] developed a deep learning-based transfer model
for a mobile ship environment. The aforementioned methods
primarily focus on developing DFL techniques that require
transferring models between a source environment and a
target environment. However, they tend to overlook the impact
of different target categories, which may cause localization
performance degradation. Wang et al. [50] investigated the
effects of target diversity on RSS measurements, and proposed
a transferring compressive-sensing-based DFL method across
different categories of targets.
In summary, transfer learning and adversarial learning based
methods have been proposed and shown to achieve satisfactory
performance in cross-domain wireless sensing tasks. How-
ever, state-of-the-art methods suffer from high computational
burden or implementation overheads. For instance, when we
want to build an effective deep learning model, there are
a large number of parameters to be tuned and the training
process is usually time-consuming due to the complicated
network architecture. Transfer learning-based methods usu-
ally need to frequently rebuild or update the existing model
when employed in new domains, making it labor-intensive.
Additionally, existing domain-independent features cannot be
directly used for DFL, and new domain-independent features
for DFL are also difficult to design. Therefore, in this contri-
bution, we consider DFL as a domain-adaptation problem, and
develop a modified online modelling framework to enhance the
robustness of DFL. This technique is able to quickly update
radio maps and associated DFL models while requiring fewer
computational resources.
III. PROBLEM FORMULATION
In this section, we first analyze two of the principle factors
which degrade the localization performance of DFL in indoor
environments, namely multipath and environmental variations.
Additionally, we present some empirical studies to motivate
the problem formulation.
A. Multipath Environments
Wi-Fi-based DFL relies on analyzing the signal variations
caused by the target to derive the fingerprint-location map-
pings. It then estimates the target’s location using a DFL
model created with the radio map. The key to such a set
of solutions is that the disturbance of Wi-Fi signals, caused
by the target’s existence, should be distinguishable. It means
that high-quality fingerprints convey more useful information
about the target’s location than low-quality fingerprints. How-
ever, the bandwidth of commodity Wi-Fi devices is limited,
typically in the order of 20 MHz or 40 MHz, making the
fingerprints obtained at different locations indistinguishable
in multipath-rich environments [51], [52]. It should be noted
that this phenomenon has been defined as the fingerprint
vanishing [53]. Understanding this phenomenon is essential
as it directly affects the effectiveness of DFL methods.
Fig. 1 depicts the results of empirical studies of DFL for
one target that considered different antenna combinations in
an indoor environment (floorplan of the environment refers
to Fig. 7 (a)). Specifically, we deployed one pair of Wi-
Fi transceiver. The Wi-Fi transmitter was equipped with two
antennas denoted by T1 and T2, and the Wi-Fi receiver was
equipped with three antennas denoted by R1, R2 and R3,
respectively. We sampled 200 times at each reference point.
According to Fig. 1, the fingerprint similarities at different
locations are high even under different antenna combinations,
indicating the severe fingerprint vanishing. In our empirical
studies, we utilized CSI amplitude, CSI conjugate multiplica-
tion (CSI-CM) [54] and CSI ratio [55] as the base signals. It
should be noted that both CSI-CM and CSI ratio offer higher
signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) than the raw CSI. We randomly
selected eight reference points, and calculated the CSI-CM
and CSI ratio using the raw CSI measurements from these
reference points. CSI and its variants are inherently complex,
containing both amplitude and phase information. As shown
in Fig. 2, the CSI amplitude, CSI-CM and CSI ratio-based
fingerprints were projected onto the complex plane to preserve
the critical information, providing a better demonstration of
the fingerprint distribution of these reference points. From
Fig. 2, we observe that different samples for the same reference
point are widely dispersed, while the samples of different
reference points are very close to each other, indicating that the
fingerprint vanishing problem is significant. Furthermore, due
to the multipath nature of Wi-Fi signal propagation, changes
in the layout of the environment may also cause variations in

B. Variations of Environments
Wi-Fi signals propagate via multiple paths traveling from
the transmitter to the receiver. When the target moves to
different locations, it can influence specific signal paths due
to reflection, diffraction, and scattering, etc., causing changes
in Wi-Fi signals. Theoretically, we can estimate the target’s
location by modelling the fingerprint-location mappings. Due
to the multipath propagation in indoor environments, the
received CSI is
H(f, t) = Hs(f) + Hd(f, t) + ∆(f, t),
(1)
where Hs(f) and Hd(f, t) represent the static and dynamic
components of the signal, and ∆(f, t) is the measurement
noise, respectively.
According to [56], when the noise is large, the received
CSI will be significantly different from the theoretical CSI.
Therefore, the CSI variation caused by the target’s existence
may be overwhelmed by the noise, which has a negative effect
on sensing SNR (SSNR). Previous works have demonstrated
that SSNR is the key to determining the sensing ability and
sensing coverage, thus noise hinders the ability to create
distinguishable fingerprints when constructing high-fidelity
radio maps.
Additionally, the characteristics of the noise, layout of the
environment, and functioning state of Wi-Fi devices (such as
aging, faults and thermal drifts, etc.) change over time, but
most existing DFL methods are developed for data collected
at a fixed time. The variations of the environment may
vary the statistical characteristics of CSI measurements, thus
DFL models without domain-adaptation ability cannot achieve

satisfactory localization performance. Fig. 3 compares the

In the empirical studies, we first used these methods to

other times. The primary reason for this is that the Wi-Fi
devices operated for more than 10 hours, the aging effect may
vary the fingerprint-location mappings. These observations
highlight the necessity of developing an online learning-based
DFL model to address the challenges.

B. Autoencoder with Online Feature Extraction Ability
An AE is a kind of unsupervised neural network, consisting
of an encoder and a decoder [57], [58]. The encoder is used to
extract features by transferring the input to the hidden layer,
while the decoder aims at reconstructing the input based on
the representations received from the encoder. This enables the
input of the AE to be completely reconstructed at the output
to achieve compact features and maintain most of the useful
information. Conventional AE is built based on the back propa-
gation (BP) method, which may inherit some of the drawbacks
of gradient-based techniques, such as achieving local optimum
and suffering from a time-consuming iterative training process.
Differently, ELM-AE utilizes randomly mapped outputs as the
latent representation, then reconstruction of the input can be
achieved through solving the least square optimization [59],
[60]. To empower the online feature extraction ability of ELM-
AE, OS-ELM is employed as a replacement for ELM in AE
training, and accordingly referred to as OS-ELM-AE (see the
upper part of Fig. 5). OS-ELM-AE, which involves the initial-
ization stage and sequential learning stage, randomly initializes
its hidden layer parameters, and can be directly updated with
new collected data without the need for retraining.

C. Fingerprint Augmentation Using Online Deep Learning
As shown in Fig. 5, OS-ML-ELM is hierarchically stacked
using OS-ELM-AEs. During the stacking process, OS-ELM-
AEs are first initialized with the CSI measurements from a

thus all the hidden layer parameters of OS-ML-ELM should
contain location-related information. We utilize such hidden
layer parameters to augment the raw fingerprints, achieving a
more accurate representation of Wi-Fi signal variations caused
by the presence of the target [62].

In this section, we first discuss the limitations of the pro-
posed framework and explore potential improvements for OS-
ML-ELM-based fingerprint augmentation and OS-ELM-FF-
based location estimation. Additionally, some future research
directions are then presented.
A. Limitations of OS-ELM-FF and Potential Improvements
The proposed OS-ELM-FF addresses the effects of outdated
data on the localization performance during the model updat-
ing process through the forgetting mechanism. However, it

cannot assess whether new sequential data will enhance the
localization performance of the existing DFL model. That is
to say, the OS-ELM-FF-based DFL model at a given time
may already capture environmental variations, making further
updates unnecessary in some cases. Therefore, an adaptive

Relevant data could be integrated into the DFL model to
further boost dynamic tracking abilities, while irrelevant data
would be directly discarded. Additionally, the OS-ELM-FF
network architecture remains fixed once the DFL model is
initialized, which may not be optimal as new sequential data
is incorporated into the model. Therefore, developing a novel
method to automatically adjust the network architecture during
the model updating process can further enhance the model’s
robustness.
OS-ML-ELM is constructed by stacking OS-ELM-AEs, but
it does not specifically address designing an optimal network
architecture or selecting parameters for each hidden layer.
The hidden layer parameters in OS-ELM-AE are generated
randomly, leading to potentially varied contributions from
different hidden nodes to fingerprint augmentation. As shown
in Fig. 17, this study could be extended by enhancing network
compactness through the selection of the most relevant hidden
nodes to represent the overall hidden nodes using dimen-
sionality reduction techniques, such as principal components
analysis (PCA).
B. Framework Scalability and Adaptability
The proposed online data-driven modelling framework aims
to address a critical challenge: How to enhance the perfor-
mance of wireless sensing systems with data collected at
different times in an online setting. In this study, we use DFL
as a case study to demonstrate the effectiveness and feasibility
of the proposed framework. In fact, the proposed framework
is scalable and can be modified for other wireless sensing
applications. Each module in the proposed framework can be
adjusted, replaced, or expanded to meet the specific needs
of various wireless sensing applications. For instance, in the
fingerprint augmentation, OS-ML-ELM could be replaced with
a generative adversarial network (GAN) to extract domain-
independent features [27], [74]. Furthermore, the proposed
framework has the potential to incorporate advanced ma-
chine/deep learning algorithms with domain-adaptation capa-

bilities, as well as more sophisticated learning paradigms to
address rapid and drastic environmental dynamics. Integrating
methods such as meta learning and transfer learning into the
online learning-based DFL model will further enhance the
robustness under varying environmental conditions [75].
Additionally, the fingerprint augmentation and location es-
timation in the proposed framework primarily relies on data-
driven modelling. As such, this can occasionally result in
physically inconsistent and implausible location estimations.
In the next stage of this work, we will study the integration
of fundamental physical laws and domain knowledge into the
online learning-based fingerprint augmentation and location
estimation processes [76], [77]. By incorporating observa-
tional, empirical, physical or mathematical insights related to
the wireless signal propagation, the aim is to regularize the
data-driven models, improving the overall performance of DFL
systems.
C. Challenges in Mobile Environments
Most existing DFL methods assume a static scenario where
Wi-Fi devices remain fixed. However, the widespread use
of mobile communication devices, such as smartphones and
smartwatches, has led to an increasing prevalence of mobile
receivers [78]. Conventional DFL methods designed for sta-
tionary transceivers may struggle to accurately map signal
variations to a target’s location, even with minor changes in
Wi-Fi device placement. The proposed framework leverages
the online learning-based fingerprint augmentation and target
location estimation, effectively mitigating the impact of device
mobility and enhancing localization performance.
D. Comparative Advantages Over Traditional Methods
While some baseline methods such as SVM achieve rea-
sonable localization accuracy, they fail to maintain consistent
performance over time and across different environmental
conditions [79], [80]. The proposed framework can effec-
tively adapt to temporal shifts over hours and days. Com-
pared to methods with domain-adaptation ability, one of the
major advantages of the proposed framework is its ability
to continuously adapt without requiring periodic retraining.
This significantly reduces the cost of maintaining large-scale
DFL systems and makes deployment in scenarios where the
constitution of the environment is subject to change feasible.
Unlike baseline methods, which need extensive labeled data
for every new condition or configuration, our DFL model
self-updates in an online manner, making it highly practical
for real-world applications. The proposed framework is an
initial attempt to enhance the localization performance through
feature augmentation and self-updating, providing a general
online learning methodology for both DFL and other wireless
sensing applications.
VII. CONCLUSION
This study has developed a novel online data-driven mod-
elling framework for DFL robustness enhancement in different
domains. An OS-ML-ELM stacked by OS-ELM-AEs was first
employed for fingerprint augmentation to alleviate the effects
of the fingerprint vanishing on the localization performance.
It was shown that OS-ELM-AE can be directly updated using
new data without the need for retraining, meaning that the
radio map constructed by the augmented fingerprints can
be directly updated. To further strengthen the localization
performance, an OS-ELM-FF-based DFL model was designed
for domain-adaptation ability enhancement. Similar to the
online representation of fingerprints, the OS-ELM-FF-based
DFL model can also be directly updated with data collected
from other domains. The forgetting mechanism utilized in OS-
ELM-FF enabled new sequential data to make enhanced con-
tributions during the model updating process, while reducing
the effects of outdated data. Critically, it was also shown to
accelerate the model updating. Results of extensive experi-
ments in different environments and scenarios have verified
the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed framework.

Abstract: Wi-Fi-based device-free localization (DFL) will be an integral part of many emerging applications, such as smart healthcare and smart homes. One popular approach to DFL in Wi-Fi makes use of fingerprinting based on channel state information (CSI). Unfortunately, high-quality fingerprints can- not easily be obtained in many real-world environments due to the complicated, time-varying and multipath conditions which exist. Additionally, existing methods struggle to update the DFL models in a real-time manner to track changes of environment. To address these issues, an online data-driven modelling DFL framework is designed for robustness enhancement. Specifically, the raw CSI data is first augmented with the hidden layer parameters of an online deep neural network to strengthen the pair-to-pair mappings between signal variations and a target’s location. The radio map created with the augmented fingerprints can be updated with new sequential data collected from other domains, such as different times and layouts of the same envi- ronment. Subsequently, a novel online DFL model is established using these augmented fingerprints, which itself can be updated with new sequential data from other domains without the need for retraining. A forgetting mechanism is considered to mitigate the effects of outdated data on the localization performance. To validate our new framework, a comprehensive set of experiments have been performed in various environments for different scenarios. The experimental results verify the robustness and responsive tracking ability of the proposed online data-driven modelling DFL framework.
